title: Negation
description: Understand clausal and subclausal negation, scope and focus, polarity-sensitive items, multiple negation and negative concord.
example: He didn’t read the report, not even the summary.

key_terms.definition: The contrast between positive and negative clauses.
Negation that makes the whole clause negative.
Negation that affects a constituent without making the whole clause negative.
Negation marked in association with the verb, often with not or n’t.
Negation marked on a dependent rather than on the verb.
Negation marked by a dedicated negative word such as not or no.
Negation marked by a word or affix with another function as well, such as never or un-.
A negator meaning zero or none, such as no, none, never, neither or nor.
A word located towards the negative end of a scale, such as few, hardly or rarely.
Negation marked by a prefix or suffix, such as un-, non- or -less.
Negation used to reject a formulation, implicature or pronunciation rather than the truth of a proposition.
The part of the meaning that is negated.
The part of the scope that is most prominently negated.
An expression such as any, ever or at all that is favoured in negative or non-affirmative contexts.
An expression such as some or already that is favoured in positive contexts.
A question, conditional, comparative or other context that is not a positive assertion.
An idiom with a negative meaning that is not simply a polarity-sensitive item, such as not lift a finger.
The marking of a single semantic negation more than once, as in non-standard I didn’t say nothing.
A negative marker that adds no separate semantic negation.
Negation understood in an embedded clause even when marked in the matrix.
A tag whose polarity is opposite to that of the clause it follows.
A reduced negative response that rejects a proposition or proposal.
Not used as a pro-form for a negative clause, as in I think not.
A negative expression used to convey a positive meaning indirectly, as in not uncommon.

intro: *He didn’t read the report, not even the summary.* Take the second half away and the sentence still stands; keep it, and the denial reaches down to the smallest item. That one small word can do more than deny a proposition. It can cancel an implication, reject a pronunciation, or stand in for a whole clause that nobody wants to repeat.

The description begins with the tests that separate a negative clause from a positive one, then sorts negation along four contrasts: verbal and non-verbal, analytic and synthetic, clausal and subclausal, ordinary and metalinguistic. From there it turns to approximate and affixal negators, to the items that live only in negative or non-affirmative company, and to the questions of scope and focus that decide what a negative actually denies. Multiple negation, negative concord, metalinguistic correction, responses with *so* and *not*, and the rhetorical use of negation bring the chapter to a close.
The question worth asking is not whether a word is negative. It is how far the negative reaches, which element it throws into relief, and whether it turns the whole clause or only a phrase inside it.

blocks.text: Set *It is raining* beside *It isn’t raining* and the difference looks like one word. The two clauses then part company in ways that have nothing to do with weather: they accept different continuations, different tags, different connectives. Positive is the simpler case, the one a description can take for granted; almost everything interesting happens on the negative side.

Four continuations expose the difference. A negative clause tolerates a *not even* supplement and takes *neither* or *nor* where a positive clause wants *so*. Its tag reverses polarity, and a negative constituent moved to the front drags the auxiliary with it. The table below sets the four side by side, each row pairing a negative clause with its positive counterpart.

No single test settles the matter. Inversion also follows *so* and *only*, and same-polarity tags turn up with their own pragmatic point. The tests are strongest as a set, and strongest of all when a clause is placed next to its positive counterpart and the two are made to behave differently.

blocks.text: *He doesn’t dine out* and *He never dines out* deny the same habit, but the negative has moved: in the first it hangs on the auxiliary, in the second on the adverb. That is one contrast among several. A description of negation needs more than one axis; the one used here has four.

*He doesn’t dine out* puts the negative on the auxiliary; *He never dines out* puts it on a dependent. Two of the axes concern form. Verbal negation attaches *not* or *n’t* to the verb or its auxiliary and calls on *do* when no auxiliary is there; non-verbal negation puts the negative on a dependent, as *never* and *nothing* do. Analytic negation uses a marker whose only job is negation, while synthetic negation uses a word or affix that does something else as well — *never* carries time, *un-* builds an adjective. The axes cross: *He never dines out* is non-verbal and synthetic at once.

*We were friends at no time* denies a friendship and behaves like any negative clause. *We were friends in no time* says the friendship formed quickly, and the clause itself is positive, because the negative is walled up inside a phrase. The other two axes concern meaning. Ordinary negation denies that something is so. Metalinguistic negation objects to how something was put: *Max hasn’t got four children, he’s got five* does not deny the four so much as the suggestion that four is the end of the count.

Metalinguistic: Max hasn’t got four children; he’s got five.

blocks.text: English verbs do not inflect for negation. There is no form *readn’t*, no negative ending on *read*. What the grammar does instead is attach *not* to the first auxiliary, and when a clause has no auxiliary it presses *do* into service to carry tense and agreement: *He is not ready*, *They have not finished*, *He didn’t read it*.

The imperative makes its own arrangements. *Be late* has no auxiliary, yet its negative is *Don’t be late*; *Be not late* survives only as archaism or literary flourish. Negative imperatives are a construction in their own right, not declaratives with the subject deleted.

Non-finite clauses take *not* without *do*. In a *to*-infinitival the marker normally comes before *to*, though a split infinitive puts it after; gerund-participials and subjunctives place it before the verb. None of these constructions accepts dummy *do*, and the examples below show the three shapes.

items.text: It seemed unwise not to answer.

items.text: Not having read the report, she said nothing.
items.note: Gerund-participial with initial not.

items.text: It is essential that he not be told.
items.note: Subjunctive with not before the plain verb.

blocks.text: *Not happy* is the clearest case: the negative sits on an adjective, and the clause around it can stay positive. The same marker can be aimed at a quantifier, at an adverb, or at a preposition phrase, leaving the rest of the clause untouched. *No* works differently, doing negation and determination at once, which is why *no money* and *no excuses* need no separate *not*.

The absolute negators mean zero or none, and they differ more in grammar than in meaning. *No* is a determinative. *None* stands alone, often as a fused head, as in *None of them came*. *Nobody*, *nothing* and *nowhere* are compounds. *Never* belongs here too, though its meaning leans on time and frequency as much as on absence.

Some of these forms negate a clause and some only a phrase, and the surface does not show which. *I saw nothing* denies that any seeing took place, exactly as *I didn’t see anything* does. *We were friends in no time* contains the same negative word but describes a quick friendship; the clause passes the tests for a positive, because the negative is sealed inside the phrase.

Between the two lies the idiom. *He is no fool* can deny foolishness outright or offer a wry compliment, and only context and intonation decide which. Here the negator is doing lexical work, not clause-level work.

items.note: Not negates the quantifier many.
Non-verbal clausal negation with nothing.

This is typically an idiomatic assessment, often subclausal.

blocks.text: Not every negative sits at zero. *Few*, *little*, *barely*, *hardly*, *scarcely*, *rarely* and *seldom* place a situation near the bottom of a scale and leave the possibility of some. *Few of them supported her* suggests that a handful did, yet the clause still behaves as negative in the polarity tests; approximation and polarity are separate matters.
The indefinite article makes the difference plain. *A few people came* reports that some came; *Few people came* reports that not many did. The same reversal separates *a little* from *little*.

Affixal negation works inside a word: *unhappy*, *intolerant*, *non-negotiable*, *careless*. Because the negative never reaches clause level, the clause itself counts as positive and takes a negative tag. *These terms are non-negotiable, aren’t they?* is therefore normal, while *These terms aren’t negotiable, are they?* belongs to the verbal pattern.

*Unhappy* is a lexical item with its own degree and colour, not simply the syntactic negation of *happy*; *not common* and *uncommon* differ in strength and register. Treating an affix as a compressed *not* misses the point. *Not unattractive* shows what happens when a negative is allowed to stand in front of a positive adjective: the result is litotes, an indirect and usually weaker positive.

Positive orientation: some people came.

items.text: These terms are non-negotiable, aren’t they?

blocks.text: *I didn’t see anything* is unremarkable. *I saw anything* is not English. The word *any* seems to need a negative or a question somewhere near it, and the same holds for *ever*, *yet*, *at all*, *any longer* and idioms such as *lift a finger* and *sleep a wink*. These are negative polarity items, and they are not equally strong: *any* is the weakest, *at all* adds emphasis, and the idioms are more emphatic still.

*Any* turns up in questions, conditionals, comparatives, *before* clauses, *only*, *few*, and the complements of *doubt*, *deny* and *surprise*, not just under negation. Negation is only the most conspicuous licensor. What unites these contexts is not a single negative word but a shared failure to assert: each leaves a proposition open, denied, or merely supposed. The examples below arrange several of them side by side.

*Not lift a finger* has a fixed negative meaning and very little internal variation; *any* is a quantifier with a wide distribution across contexts. An idiom is not just a strong NPI. One is a lexical item with a negative cast, the other a polarity-sensitive word that the grammar licenses.

blocks.text: *I have already eaten* passes without comment. *I haven’t already eaten* does not; it wants a contrast, a correction, or a very specific tone. *Already* is a positive polarity item, and it keeps company with *some*, *still*, *somewhat*, *rather* and *pretty*. The restriction is a strong tendency, not an absolute law, and a cooperative context can override it.

Put a PPI under negation and it usually needs a special reading. *I don’t have some money* is odd unless *some* is contrastive: not money in general, but some particular sum. *She isn’t still here* is easier, because *still* can fall under the scope of the negative and yield the reading ‘she is no longer here’. The label matters less than the scope relation.

Questions, conditionals, comparatives, *before* clauses, *only*, *few*, and the complements of *doubt*, *deny* and *surprise* all qualify as non-affirmative. The wider environment is easier to list than to define. These contexts resemble one another family by family rather than sharing a single semantic feature.

Yet is the negative-context counterpart.

blocks.text: *Liz didn’t delete the backup file* denies a whole event: no deletion of that file by Liz took place. The scope of the negative is the proposition, and the focus is the part the denial lands on hardest. Stress can move that focus without changing the syntax: *Liz* didn’t delete the file, or she didn’t delete *the backup file*.

Removing the negative gives a rough test. The positive counterpart of the sentence is *Liz deleted the backup file*, and the negative denies exactly that. Apply the same procedure to *Not many people came* and the result differs: what is denied is the size of the crowd, not the arrival of any people at all. Two negatives, two scopes.

Scope also shifts under quantifiers, modals and reason clauses. *Not all the students passed* denies a universal; *All the students didn’t pass* can deny the universal or report a universal failure, depending on where the negative is understood. A *because* clause is just as slippery: *I didn’t buy it because it was expensive* can give the reason for not buying or deny that the price was the reason.

blocks.text: *Mary doesn’t like you* usually means something stronger than its literal content: that Mary dislikes you. Strictly, it is true if she has no feelings either way, and a flat denial can cancel the inference. *He doesn’t have many friends* works the same way, implicating a small circle without quite saying so. Negative clauses tend to be read towards the more specific, more informative end of what they allow.

Medium-strength predicates produce a related effect. *I don’t want to hear about it* is normally heard as *I want not to hear about it*, with the negative transplanted into the subordinate clause. *I don’t think she’s coming* leans towards *I think she isn’t coming*. In both, the negative is written in the matrix and understood in the complement.

The effect depends on strength. *I’m not willing to be included* entails *I’m willing not to be included*, so no implicature is needed. *I don’t insist on being included* does not suggest *I insist on not being included*; *insist* is too strong to let the negative slide downward. *Want*, *advise*, *likely*, *think*, *believe* and *seem* occupy the middle ground, while *know* and *insist* sit outside it.

Modals can build subordinate negation into their meaning rather than leaving it to inference. *You mustn’t tell anyone* says that you are obliged not to tell, with the negative inside the complement of *must*. *You needn’t tell anyone* says that no obligation applies, with the negative outside. Scope explains the contrast, and it survives even when the two forms sound equally forbidding.

items.note: Implicates that Mary dislikes you, but does not entail it.

items.text: I don’t want to hear about it.

blocks.text: Two negative words in one clause can mean two denials or one. *I didn’t say I didn’t want it* contains two separate negations, one in the matrix and one in the complement, and they do not cancel. Non-standard *He didn’t say nothing* contains two negative markers but a single denial: he said nothing. The first pattern is multiple semantic negation; the second is negative concord.

Standard English has small pockets of concord of its own. *Neither illegal nor immoral* marks both coordinates and negates once. A negative parenthetical can double the marking without doubling the meaning, as in *They aren’t here, I don’t think*. And a subordinate clause after *I wouldn’t be surprised if* may carry a negative that adds nothing at all, a pleonastic marker rather than a second denial.

Cockney and African American Vernacular English regularly use *He didn’t say nothing* for a single negation. Concord is regular in many non-standard varieties, and it is not a lapse in logic. The rule that two negatives cancel belongs to semantic negation, not to the number of negative words a grammar allows. Italian and Spanish mark a single negation more than once in much the same way.

blocks.text: *She didn’t have lunch with my old man: she had lunch with my father.* The denial is not aimed at the lunch. It objects to the phrase *my old man*, and the correction supplies a more acceptable wording. This is metalinguistic negation: a negative that rejects a formulation, an implicature or a pronunciation rather than the truth of a proposition.

The classic case targets an implicature. *Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got five* would contradict itself if *not* denied the proposition outright, because a man with five children has four as well. What is rejected is the suggestion that four is the upper limit. *Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got three* is ordinary negation by comparison, denying the count itself.

Metalinguistic negatives tend to sound different. They carry a marked intonation, often a fall-rise on the offending item, and they invite a correction. The target can be a word, a pronunciation, a register or a presupposition, and the negative is doing corrective work rather than descriptive work.

sections.title: Responses and anaphoric so and not

blocks.text: *Isn’t it ready?* can be answered with *Yes* to confirm readiness or *No* to deny it, and the same words can confirm or reject depending on which proposition the speaker takes as the anchor. Answers to polar questions are shaped by the polarity of the question and by what the answerer wants to do with it. Agreement and disagreement are not the same as yes and no.

*So* and *not* work as pro-forms for whole clauses. *I think so* stands in for a positive complement; *I think not* stands in for a negative one. *I was told so* and *I was told not* show the same division. In these uses *not* is a complement, not a modifier hovering near the verb.

Preposed adverbs and preposition phrases can accompany the pro-form, but not symmetrically. *Apparently so* and *Apparently not* both work. *On the whole not* is possible; *On the whole so* is not. The difference follows from the different syntactic status of the two pro-forms in reduced clauses.

items.text: Are they reliable? I think so.
items.note: So stands for the positive proposition.

items.text: Are they reliable? I think not.
items.note: Not stands for the negative proposition.
An adverb can accompany so.
A PP can accompany not, but not so in the same way.

blocks.text: *I didn’t buy it because it was expensive* can give the price as the reason for not buying, or deny that the price was the reason. Negation is a reliable source of ambiguity in writing because its scope is often invisible. *All that glitters is not gold* can mean that nothing glittering is gold or that not everything glittering is. Word order alone does not settle either case; scope and focus do.

Negative concord attracts social judgement out of proportion to its linguistic interest. It is a regular feature of many dialects and follows its own rules. Formal Standard English can use multiple semantic negation for emphasis or contradiction, but the result needs a context strong enough to keep the two denials apart.

Litotes turns negation into indirect praise or criticism: *not uncommon*, *not unattractive*, *not a little worried*. The figure softens a claim or shades it with irony, and its effect depends on the scale and on what the reader expects. Pushed too far, the negative goes vague, and the reader stops being able to measure the positive behind it.

items.text: All that glitters is not gold.
items.note: Ambiguous between universal and non-universal scope.

items.text: I didn’t buy it because it was expensive.
items.note: The reason clause can fall inside or outside the scope of negation.

blocks.text: The four contrasts — verbal and non-verbal, analytic and synthetic, clausal and subclausal, ordinary and metalinguistic — give the description its axes. Nothing about negation is settled by a single word. The polarity tests decide whether a clause as a whole is negative.

Verbal negation puts *not* or *n’t* on a primary verb and uses *do*-support where no auxiliary exists. Non-verbal negation covers *not* with a constituent, absolute negators such as *no* and *never*, approximate negators such as *few* and *hardly*, and affixes. Polarity-sensitive items distribute across positive, negative and non-affirmative contexts, and those contexts form a family rather than a single class.

Scope and focus explain how one negative form can deny different things, and multiple negation divides into separate denials and concord. Metalinguistic negation corrects formulations and implicatures rather than facts. *So* and *not* supply pro-forms for the clauses that would otherwise have to be repeated.

blocks.title: A negation checklist
blocks.text: Identify the negative marker. Decide whether it is verbal or non-verbal, analytic or synthetic. Test whether the clause is negative or only a constituent. Then identify the scope and focus, and check whether the negation is ordinary or metalinguistic.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly describes clausal negation?

options.text: It makes the whole clause negative and passes the polarity tests.
options.feedback: Subclausal negation does not make the clause negative.

options.text: It is always marked by an affix.
options.feedback: Affixal negation is subclausal.

options.text: It always contains two negative words.
options.feedback: One negative marker is enough.

worked: Take *He didn’t read the report, not even the summary*. The finite clause is negative: it takes the *not even* continuation, would take *neither* rather than *so*, and takes the reversed tag *did he?*. The negative is verbal, marked on the auxiliary *did*, and it has scope over the proposition that he read the report.

The phrase *not even the summary* is a detached supplement, not part of the core clause. It identifies a more specific focus for the negation: the report was not read, and even the summary was not read. The example shows how a negative clause can combine clause-level polarity with a focused supplement.
application: Start with the negative marker and identify what it is attached to. If it is on the verb or an auxiliary, the negation is verbal. If it is on an NP, AdjP, AdvP or PP, it may be non-verbal and possibly subclausal.
Next, test the clause. Does it allow not even? Does it take neither or so? Which tag does it take? Does a prenuclear negative trigger inversion? These tests separate clausal from subclausal negation.

Then identify scope and focus. Remove the negative and compare the positive counterpart. Decide which part of the proposition is denied and which element is most prominent. Finally, check whether the negation is ordinary or metalinguistic, and whether multiple negative markers express one semantic negation or several.
reveal: In *He didn’t read the report, not even the summary*, the negative is verbal and clausal: it is marked on the auxiliary *did* and denies the proposition that he read the report. *Not even the summary* is a focused supplement that strengthens the negation by extending it to a minimal case.
recap: Polarity is a clause-level property with syntactic tests. Negation can be verbal or non-verbal, analytic or synthetic, clausal or subclausal, ordinary or metalinguistic. Scope and focus determine what the negative actually denies.

NPIs and PPIs are licensed by positive, negative and non-affirmative contexts. Multiple negative markers can express several negations or a single negation with concord. Metalinguistic negation rejects formulations and implicatures rather than truth.

self_check.question: Name the four tests for clause polarity.
self_check.answer: Not even continuation, neither/nor versus so, reversed-polarity tags, and inversion with a prenuclear negative.

self_check.question: What is the difference between clausal and subclausal negation?
self_check.answer: Clausal negation makes the whole clause negative and passes the polarity tests; subclausal negation affects a constituent without making the clause negative.

self_check.question: What is the difference between an NPI and a negative idiom?
self_check.answer: An NPI is licensed by negative or non-affirmative contexts; a negative idiom has a fixed negative meaning and limited variation.

self_check.question: What is negative concord?
self_check.answer: The marking of a single semantic negation more than once, as in non-standard He didn’t say nothing.

self_check.question: What is metalinguistic negation?
self_check.answer: Negation used to reject a formulation, implicature or pronunciation rather than the truth of a proposition.

opening.prompt: Which item is a negative polarity item?

closing.prompt: Why is We were friends in no time not a negative clause?

options.text: It means “very quickly” and does not pass the clause-polarity tests.
options.feedback: The negation is confined to the phrase.
It contains no, but the negation is subclausal.
The tag reflects the subclausal meaning.

closing.prompt: Why does Don’t be late require do?

options.text: Imperative negation uses do even when the positive contains be.
options.feedback: The imperative is a distinct construction.
Be is an auxiliary even as a copula.
The complement does not determine do-support.

closing.prompt: Why does non-negotiable take a negative tag?

options.text: Affixal negation is subclausal, so the clause remains positive.
options.feedback: The negative is inside the adjective.
It is a prefix.
Negotiable is positive.

closing.prompt: What does I don’t want to hear about it typically implicate?

options.text: I want not to hear about it.
options.feedback: This is the medium-strength subordinate negation implicature.

options.text: I am indifferent about hearing it.
options.feedback: That is compatible with the sentence but not the usual implicature.

options.text: I insist on not hearing about it.
options.feedback: Insist is stronger than want.

options.text: Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got five.

options.text: Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got three.
options.feedback: That is ordinary negation.
That is ordinary negation.
